title: Give us a king (1 Samuel 8)
hookLine: the people want a king like everyone else, and are warned what kings take
last: LET NONE OF HIS WORDS FALL TO THE GROUND.

lines: HIS SONS WALKED NOT IN HIS WAYS.
cards: The boy who answered in the night is an old man now, and the story repeats in a way that stings.
Samuel makes his sons judges, and "his sons walked not in his ways, but turned aside after lucre, and took bribes, and perverted judgment." Eli's sons all over again.
So the elders of Israel come to Samuel at Ramah with a reasonable request: you're old, your sons aren't like you, "now make us a king to judge us like all the nations."
And the text says, simply, "the thing displeased Samuel."

teach.b: Samuel prays, and God's answer surprises twice. First: give them what they ask.

"Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee: for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected me, that I should not reign over them." It isn't about you, Samuel. Second: warn them first.
Samuel's speech is blunt, and its key word is take.
"He will take your sons" for his chariots, his horsemen, his fields, his weapons. "He will take your daughters to be confectionaries, and to be cooks, and to be bakers."
Your best fields, a tenth of your grain and flocks, your servants, your donkeys. "And ye shall be his servants." One day you'll cry out because of the king you chose.

teach.h: NAY; BUT WE WILL HAVE A KING.
teach.b: The people don't argue with a single point: "Nay; but we will have a king over us; That we also may be like all the nations; and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles."
Like all the nations, again. They heard every cost and still chose to belong. God tells Samuel, make them a king.

teach.h: READERS HEAR IT MORE THAN ONE WAY.
teach.b: Readers hear this chapter more than one way. Some hear a warning against kingship itself, or against any power that only takes.
Others point out that Deuteronomy had already allowed for a king, and that the trouble was the reason: to be like everyone else.
Christian readers also follow this road on to David and a promised throne, and to Jesus called the son of David. The chapter ends with the request granted, and the warning on the record.

how: Christians read 1 Samuel 8 in different ways, as a warning about power and as part of the long road to King David, and some read it when thinking about how much to borrow from the culture around them.

games.q: you're one of the elders. Samuel has just told you a king will take your sons, your daughters, your fields and a tenth of your grain. what do you say?
o: nay; we will have a king, like all the nations.
let's ask for a king with limits.
games.why: they hear every cost and choose it anyway, that we also may be like all the nations (8:19–20).

practice: Think of one thing you want right now mostly because others have it: a phone, a look, a kind of house, a stance online.
Don't judge it yet; just ask Samuel's question, what will it take, and let the list come: your time, your money, your attention, your quiet. If you pray, bring that wanting to God as it is.

wordCard.voice: Ramah. The town where Israel's elders came to Samuel and asked for a king to judge and lead them like all the nations, after hearing everything a king would take.

orig.note: Hebrew: king. the word the elders ask for in 1 Samuel 8:5.

carryVoice: Your line: not like the nations. Belonging can cost more than it appears. See you tomorrow.
